interactions.summary: Jiang closes by presenting Dante as a divinely tasked messenger whose biographical hardship and world-historical impact make accidental genius look implausible.
A student pushes back with a humanist objection, arguing that divine explanation diminishes Dante's own greatness and is unnecessary for appreciating the poem.

Jiang accepts the student's point at one level but reframes the class as an exercise in leap-of-faith speculation, claiming that full entry into the Divine Comedy requires risking belief in its divinity.

claims.claim: Jiang says Dante died in exile, lived on patronage, finished the Divine Comedy in 1321, died months later, saw no fame in his lifetime, and received no payment for the poem.
claims.temporal_scope: Jiang biographical claims stated on 2026-06-16 about Dante's life.

claims.claim: Jiang says the Catholic Church was so angry at Dante that it wanted to burn his body, and he treats Dante's long labor without obvious reward as evidence of mission rather than ordinary ambition.
Jiang argues that Dante knew his mission from birth, held the Divine Comedy in fragments throughout life, and eventually wrote it once he conceived the whole.
Jiang says the Divine Comedy is the source of the Renaissance, the Protestant Reformation, the Enlightenment, and modernity itself, and he treats that scale of influence as evidence of divine design.

A student argues that this divine explanation is too absolute because it diminishes Dante and the Divine Comedy as humanist achievements, and because human beings do not need God in order to value them.
Jiang responds that the class is not an academic seminar but a journey of intellectual speculation that requires a leap of faith into the poem's divinity and perfection.

Jiang says that fully embracing the Divine Comedy as divine can transform the reader, and that the wager is asymmetrical because if the belief is false there is no harm, but if true it could become life-transforming.

signature_moments.moment: Dante is recast as a messenger who spent his whole life assembling a divinely given work before history finally recognized it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Dante was a messenger of God himself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is Jiang's final answer to why Dante alone could write this poem and why his suffering was not pointless.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang explicitly says the class is not an academic seminar but a speculative spiritual journey.
signature_moments.source_phrase: This is not an academic seminar. This is about intellectual speculation.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It names the pedagogical contract under which he wants the whole Dante course to be read.

signature_moments.moment: The lecture ends on a wager: risk full belief in divinity because if Jiang is right it may transform your life, and if he is wrong there is no loss.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if it is not true, there's actually no harm to you... this could be the most life transforming experience in your life
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It compresses the whole course into a Pascal-like invitation to read dangerously rather than safely.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's name for a class method that suspends purely academic distance and treats reading as a lived quest into the structure of the universe.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 closing packet turns the entire discussion of imagination and mission into an explicit classroom method: Dante's biography and influence justify a leap-of-faith reading that Jiang presents as potentially life-transforming.

uncertainty_notes.note: Several historical claims here are part of Jiang's rhetorical close rather than a source-critical historical apparatus, so later public use should preserve that they are his lecture claims on 2026-06-16.
